“A prisoner does not typically gain a legal right to freedom simply because the state made a clerical or calculation error,” said a criminal law professor familiar with California sentencing procedures. “The key questions are whether the sentence was lawful, how much time remains, and whether the state acted promptly after discovering the mistake.”

Defense attorneys in similar cases sometimes argue that re-incarceration after release can raise due process concerns, especially if a person has begun reintegrating into the community. But courts often allow authorities to correct sentence-computation errors, particularly when the mistake is discovered quickly.

## Victims’ families and public reaction

The case has long remained painful for relatives of victims and former law enforcement officers involved in the 1970s investigations.

A representative for Opsahl’s family said the erroneous release underscored the need for transparency in how prison sentences are calculated.

“This family has lived with the consequences of that crime for decades,” the representative said. “They deserve accurate information and accountability from the justice system.”

Supporters of Olson have argued over the years that she accepted responsibility, served significant prison time and had built a productive life before her arrest. Critics have said her years as a fugitive should remain central to how the justice system treats her case.

## Corrections officials reviewing case

California corrections officials said they were reviewing the circumstances of Olson’s release and how the error occurred.

“We are examining the sentence calculation process in this case to determine what went wrong and to prevent similar mistakes,” the CDCR spokesperson said.

Olson was expected to be transferred back to a state correctional facility while officials recalculated her remaining sentence.

Her arrest at LAX brought renewed attention to one of the longest-running criminal sagas to emerge from the domestic radical movements of the 1970s — a case that has combined political violence, fugitive life, plea bargains and decades of legal aftermath.
